questions.q: With "Sign in with Google", what does your server learn about the user's Google password?
questions.explain: The whole point of OAuth sign-in is that someone else checks the password. Your server never sees it.
options: It receives the password once and hashes it
It receives an encrypted copy of the password
Nothing: Google checks the password on its own page and only tells your server who the user is
It receives the password hash from Google

questions.q: In the authorization code flow, which part travels through the user's browser?
questions.explain: Only the code comes back through the browser (step 4). Your server then trades it, with its client secret, directly with Google (steps 5 and 6), so the token and the secret never pass through the browser.
options: The short-lived code, in the callback URL's query string

questions.q: Which order of steps is right?
questions.explain: Your server starts by redirecting to Google, gets a code back after the user approves, trades it for a token server to server, then reads the profile and creates its own session.
options: Exchange the code → redirect to Google → fetch the profile → user approves
Redirect to Google → user signs in and approves → Google redirects back with a code → exchange the code for a token → fetch the profile and start your own session
Fetch the profile → redirect to Google → exchange the code → user approves
User approves → fetch the profile → redirect to Google → exchange the code

questions.q: Your app gets a client id and a client secret from Google. Which is which?
questions.explain: The client id appears in the browser's address bar, so it cannot be secret. The client secret is like the JWT secrets: environment only, never in code or git.
options: Both are secret and live in .env only
The client id is public (it is in the step 1 URL); the client secret proves requests come from your server and lives in .env only
The client id is secret; the client secret goes in the URL

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Google's default scopes ask for who you are, your email and your name. GitHub gives no refresh tokens, Discord wants the client secret in an HTTP Basic header, and Apple has no profile endpoint at all.
options:
openid email profile
false basic undefined

openid email profile
true body https://appleid.apple.com/userinfo

openid email profile
false basic https://appleid.apple.com/auth/userinfo

questions.q: How many scopes should your app ask for?
questions.explain: Scopes are what you ask the user to allow. Asking for less means users trust you more, and a leaked token can do less.
options: All the provider offers, in case you need them later
None: scopes are optional and ignored

questions.q: How must the client secret travel in step 5?
questions.explain: URLs end up in logs and browser history. The preset's clientAuth says whether the secret goes in the body or a Basic header.
options: In the query string of the token URL
As a form field in the request body, or in an HTTP Basic Authorization header, never in a URL
In the authorization URL of step 1
In a cookie set on the user's browser

questions.q: The environment variables are not set, so the config has empty strings. What does this print?
questions.explain: The package refuses an empty client id or secret, even for step 1. It is a server configuration error, so the status is 500 and the message is hidden from clients.

questions.q: Finish googleConfig(env). Read GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID and GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET from env. If one is missing or empty, throw new Error(`${name} is not set. Add it to your .env file.`) for the first missing one. Otherwise return { provider: "google", clientId, clientSecret, allowedRedirectUris: [CALLBACK_URL] }.
questions.explain: Build the config in one place and fail loudly at start-up when a value is missing. The message names the variable, never a value. Note the program never prints the secret.
questions.expected:
GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET is not set. Add it to your .env file.
google task-api.apps.googleusercontent.com [ 'http://localhost:3000/auth/google/callback' ]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: allowedRedirectUris is an exact allow-list. Even an extra / is refused. Otherwise an attacker could make your server send users, and their codes, somewhere else.

questions.q: Finish checkRedirect(allowed, redirectUri). Return redirectUri only if it is exactly one of the allowed strings. Otherwise throw new Error("redirectUri is not allowed"). No prefix matching.
questions.explain: A check like startsWith would let the other two through. Exact matching with includes on the list is simple and safe.
questions.expected:
ok http://localhost:3000/auth/google/callback
redirectUri is not allowed
redirectUri is not allowed

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The browser sees this URL, so everything in it is public. It carries the state and the PKCE challenge, but never the client secret or the code verifier, which you keep on the server until step 5.
options:
accounts.google.com code S256
false false true

accounts.google.com code S256
false true true

accounts.google.com token plain
false false true

accounts.google.com code S256
true false true

questions.q: Finish authorizationUrl(base, clientId, redirectUri, state, challenge). Use URL and searchParams.set to add response_type=code, client_id, redirect_uri, scope=openid email, state, code_challenge and code_challenge_method=S256, in that order. Return the URL as a string. No secret goes into it.
questions.explain: searchParams.set encodes each value for you (: and / become %3A and %2F, a space becomes +). Never glue URLs together by hand.

questions.q: What attack does the state value stop?
questions.explain: Your callback URL is public. Without state, anything you then save (tasks, files) would go into the attacker's account, where they can read it. State proves the callback belongs to a login this browser started.
options: Login CSRF: an attacker sends you a callback link with their code, and you end up logged in to the attacker's account

questions.q: Where should the server keep the state until the callback?
questions.explain: If both the cookie and the query string come from the browser, an attacker controls both. Keeping the state on the server, and giving the browser only a random id, means the attacker cannot supply a matching pair.
options: In a plain cookie with the state value, compared with === to the query string
On the server, under a random login id; the browser gets only that id, in an HttpOnly cookie
In the URL of the callback

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: verifyState returns false for any difference, and also for an empty or missing value, so two empty strings never "match". It does not throw: you throw OAuthStateMismatchError yourself.

questions.q: Why does verifyState compare in constant time instead of using ===?
questions.explain: === can stop at the first different character, so a closer guess takes a tiny bit longer. A constant-time comparison always does the same work.
options: So an attacker cannot guess the state one character at a time by measuring how long the comparison takes
Because === does not work on long strings

questions.q: Finish safeEqual(a, b), a constant-time string comparison. Return false if either is not a non-empty string, or if the lengths differ. Otherwise go through every character, combine the differences with diff |= a.charCodeAt(i) ^ b.charCodeAt(i), and return diff === 0. Do not stop early.
questions.explain: ^ (XOR) is 0 only for equal characters; |= keeps any difference. Because the loop never stops early, the time does not depend on where the first difference is. Empty values never match.

questions.q: Finish takeVerifiedLogin(loginId, receivedState, now). Look up the pending login, and delete it before checking, so a callback can never be used twice. Throw new Error("OAuth state verification failed.") if there is no login, it has expired (expiresAt < now), or the state does not match. Otherwise return its codeVerifier. (A real app compares with verifyState; === keeps this exercise short.)
questions.explain: Deleting first means a replayed callback finds nothing, and so does a second try after a forged state (login-2). Every failure gives the same message, so an attacker learns nothing about which check failed.
questions.expected:
ok verifier-1
OAuth state verification failed.
OAuth state verification failed.
OAuth state verification failed.
OAuth state verification failed.
OAuth state verification failed.

questions.q: What does PKCE protect against?
questions.explain: The server keeps a random verifier and sends only its hash, the challenge. In step 5 it sends the verifier; a thief with only the code cannot.
options: A stolen code: the code travels through the browser and can leak (history, proxy logs, extensions), but without the verifier it is useless

questions.q: RFC 7636 gives an example verifier. What does this print?
questions.explain: The challenge is base64url(SHA-256(verifier)), matching the RFC's example. A generated verifier is 64 random characters, and two verifiers never give the same challenge.

questions.q: Compute a PKCE challenge in the browser. Finish challenge(verifier): hash the verifier with crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", …), turn the bytes into base64 with btoa, then make it base64url (+ → -, / → _, remove =). The RFC 7636 example must print E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM.
questions.explain: crypto.subtle.digest returns bytes; String.fromCharCode and btoa turn them into base64, and three replaces make it URL-safe. Only this hash goes into the URL, never the verifier.

questions.q: PKCE has an older plain method. Why does the package only implement S256?
questions.explain: With S256 the URL only carries a hash of the verifier, which cannot be turned back into the verifier.
options: plain sends the verifier itself in the URL, so a thief who sees the URL has it; that protects nothing
Because Google does not support PKCE
plain needs the client secret in the URL

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A verifier must be 43 to 128 characters from the unreserved alphabet (letters, digits, -, ., _, ~). "too-short" is 9 characters.

questions.q: A fake token endpoint refuses the code. What does this print?
questions.explain: Provider errors are OAuthProviderError with status 502 (Bad Gateway: a service behind you failed). The message keeps only the short OAuth error code, never the provider's free text, which here even contained the secret.

questions.q: A fake provider answers the token and profile requests. What does this print?
questions.explain: fetchUserInfo turns each provider's own profile format into one shape: providerId (Google's sub), email, emailVerified, name and avatarUrl.
options:
Bearer 3599
undefined ada@example.com true Ada Lovelace

questions.q: After step 6, how should you find the user's local account?
questions.explain: Emails change, and an unverified email proves nothing. The provider's id for the user never changes and is unique within that provider.
options: By email, because emails are unique

questions.q: Finish findOrCreateAccount(provider, profile). Key accounts by `${provider}:${profile.providerId}`. Return the existing account if there is one. Otherwise create { id: `u-${accounts.size + 1}`, email, roles: ["user"] }, where email is the profile's email only when emailVerified === true, else "". Store and return it.
questions.explain: The same id at another provider is another person, so the key includes the provider. An unverified email is not stored as the account's email, and the role is always chosen by the server.

questions.q: A GitHub login arrives with the email ada@example.com, and Ada already has a password account with that email. What should happen?
questions.explain: Anyone can create a provider account with Ada's address. Linking on a matching email alone would let them log in as Ada: an account takeover.
options: Log the GitHub user in to Ada's account, since the emails match
Do not link them automatically; linking needs a verified email and proof the user owns the existing account, for example by logging in to it first
Delete Ada's password account and keep the GitHub one

questions.q: The callback has the Google access token. What should it send the client?
questions.explain: Google's token is for Google's API. Your API trusts only tokens it issued, tied to its own session, so logout and expiry work exactly like password logins.
options: The Google access token, so the client can call your API with it
Your own token, from a session started with auth.createSessionForUser(user.id, { method: "oauth" }); the Google token is used once and thrown away
The Google refresh token, so the client can stay logged in
The client secret, so the client can log in again later

questions.q: auth.createSessionForUser checks no password. What keeps it safe in the lesson's Task API?
questions.explain: The function trusts your code, so the service makes you switch it on for the oauth method on purpose, and it still loads the user with findUserById. Never call it with a user id taken from the request: that would let anyone log in as anyone.
options: It checks the Google access token again before it creates the session
Nothing: any route may call it with the userId from the request body
It stays switched off until externalSessionMethods: ["oauth"] lists the method, it refuses unknown or deactivated users, and the callback calls it only after the state check and the code exchange

questions.q: The user pressed "Cancel" at Google, so the callback has a state but no code. What does the lesson's callback answer?
questions.explain: The callback checks the state first, then answers 400 when there is no code. A missing code is a normal user choice, not a server failure.
options: 400, "Sign-in was cancelled", after the state check

questions.q: Finish readCallback(query). query holds the callback's query values, which may be missing or not strings. Return { status: 400, error: "Sign-in was cancelled" } when code is not a non-empty string. Otherwise return { status: 200, code, state }, with state as "" when it is not a string.
questions.explain: A query value can be missing or repeated (an array), so check the type before using it. An empty state then simply fails the state check, which runs before anything reaches Google.

questions.q: The oauth_login cookie is SameSite=Lax. Is it sent when Google redirects the browser back to your callback?
questions.explain: SameSite=Lax blocks cross-site form posts but allows top-level GET navigations. That is why Apple's POST-form callback (form_post) does not carry it.
options: No, because the request comes from another site
Yes: a redirect back is a normal top-level GET navigation, which Lax cookies follow
Only if the user clicks a button

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The package allows http only for localhost, 127.0.0.1 and [::1]. A real callback must use https://, or the code could be read on the network.

questions.q: You run three servers behind a load balancer and keep pending logins in a Map. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: A Map lives in one process. Keep pending logins in a shared store, such as your database or Redis.
options: The callback may reach a different server than the start, which has no record of the login, so it fails the state check
Users are logged in three times

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: These fail before any request is made. GitHub issues no refresh tokens, Apple has no profile endpoint, and a token URL pointing at a private or cloud-metadata address is refused.

questions.q: Why does the package refuse a tokenUrl such as https://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data?
questions.explain: Server-side request forgery (SSRF) tricks a server into calling addresses only it can reach. 169.254.169.254 is where cloud machines keep their credentials.
options: Because the address is too long
Your server fetches that URL itself; a private or cloud-metadata address could make it read internal secrets (SSRF)
Because Google uses a different address
Because IP addresses are never allowed in URLs

questions.q: A GitHub profile has no public email. What does this print?
questions.explain: The id becomes a string, and GitHub's login is used as the name. The package never makes up an email, so your code must handle an account without one.

questions.q: Apple has no profile endpoint; the profile is inside the idToken from the token exchange. What must you do before trusting it?
questions.explain: Decoding a token is not verifying it: anyone can make a token with any payload. Only a checked signature proves Apple issued it.
options: Nothing: it came from Apple, so it is safe
Verify the token's signature yourself, because this package does not check it
Base64-decode it; that proves it is real
Send it to the browser to check

questions.q: A callback handler takes codeVerifier from ctx.query.verifier. What is wrong with that?
questions.explain: PKCE only helps if the verifier never leaves your server. Store it with the pending login, next to the state, and read it back in the callback.
options: Nothing, as long as it is a string
The verifier travelled through the browser next to the code, so a thief who has one has both; the verifier must stay on the server
The verifier should be in the request body instead
The verifier must be hashed first

questions.q: Like the practice's githubConfig(), this asks only for read:user. What does this print?
questions.explain: Your scopes replace the preset's defaults. searchParams.get returns decoded values, so the redirect URI prints normally. Without user:email, GitHub profiles will usually have no email.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: access_type=offline and prompt=consent come from the Google preset and make Google issue a refresh token. The URL never has a client_secret or a code_verifier.
options:
offline consent openid email profile
false false

offline consent openid email profile
true false

null null openid email profile
false true

questions.q: Google sends a profile whose email is not verified. What does this print?
questions.explain: The package passes on what the provider says: emailVerified is false. Your code then stores no email for this account, because an unverified email proves nothing about who the user is.
